vignette: Mrs. Aisha Johnson, an 80-year-old widowed African American woman and retired policy analyst, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that occurred five years ago. The event left her with vivid but fragmented memories and a heightened sense of threat in her daily environment. The accident was a turning point for Mrs. Johnson. She had been driving home on a cold evening when another car swerved into her lane, forcing her to swerve off the road. Her car hit a tree at high speed, causing significant damage and immediate pain. The smell of burnt rubber and alcohol from spilled windshield washer fluid filled the air as she lay trapped in the wreckage, shivering uncontrollably despite her warm clothing. She remembers the sudden movements of first responders pulling her out and the intense relief once they reached her. Since then, Mrs. Johnson has been acutely sensitive to specific triggers that bring back flashes of those terrifying moments. The sensation of cold on her skin immediately puts her on guard, as she associates it with the shivering she experienced post-accident. She also finds herself hypervigilant when she catches a whiff of alcohol or burnt smells, which instantly transport her back to the scene of the crash. These triggers not only evoke memories but also heighten her sense of threat. The sudden movements by others, like the swift actions of the first responders, can put her immediately on edge. Mrs. Johnson’s memory of the event is fragmented and partial. Some moments are crystal clear—such as the smell of burnt rubber and the sensation of shivering—while other parts remain a complete blank. She often finds herself pushing away these memories before she can fully recall them, making it difficult to piece together the entire experience. However, something in her surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, leaving her feeling as if the accident is happening all over again. Her heightened sense of threat has only worsened this cycle. The strong negative emotions—fear and horror—are always just below the surface. When she encounters a trigger like the smell of alcohol or burnt rubber, she becomes immediately on guard and recalls those fragmented memories with vivid intensity. These flashbacks are often accompanied by intense feelings of fear and anxiety, which further reinforce her belief that any sudden movement could be life-threatening. Her hypervigilance has significantly impacted her daily life. At home, she avoids opening windows or going out during cold weather to avoid the sensation of cold on her skin. In her former role as a policy analyst, attending meetings with large groups where people might make sudden movements became increasingly difficult. She would often leave early or find excuses not to attend, leading to strained professional relationships and reduced productivity. Mrs. Johnson had come to believe that any small trigger could lead back to the trauma of the accident, making her world feel smaller and more dangerous each day. The constant state of alertness has taken a toll on both her mental health and daily functioning. She is most afraid of losing control again, reliving those terrifying moments without warning. What finally brought Mrs. Johnson to seek help was the realization that she could no longer avoid these triggers indefinitely without it affecting her quality of life further. She hopes to regain some sense of normalcy and be able to navigate her environment without constant fear. While her fears are deeply rooted, she is eager to find ways to manage them and perhaps piece together a more coherent memory of the event that haunts her.
